feedback: If a learner says blood only carries oxygen, prompt them to add nutrients, water and the waste (carbon dioxide) it collects.
If a learner confuses arteries and veins, return them to direction: away from the heart = artery, back to the heart = vein.
For the blue-blood myth, clarify oxygen-poor blood is dark red; blue is only how diagrams, and sometimes skin/veins, can appear.
activities.intendedInsight: Each vessel's name carries its function; blood is a two-way carrier (delivers and collects); the blue colouring is only a convention, and the heart's real position and size differ from common myths.
learnerActions: Match each part (heart, artery, vein, capillary, blood) to its job.
Explain why blood keeps going round instead of stopping, and list what blood carries (oxygen, nutrients and water delivered to cells; carbon dioxide and other waste carried away from them).
Decide whether this statement is true: 'the blood in your veins is blue' — and explain your answer.

Locate roughly where the heart sits (near the middle of the chest behind the breastbone, tilted slightly to the left, about fist-sized), correcting the idea that it is on the far left or heart-shaped.
activities.title: Name the parts and bust the myths

feedback: If a learner says the heart makes new blood, separate 'pump' from 'produce': the heart moves blood; blood cells are made in bone marrow.
If the described path has no return, prompt them to trace blood back through the veins — it's a closed circuit, not an open one.
If capillaries are omitted so the loop has a gap, point out capillaries join arteries to veins and are where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged with cells.
If only oxygen is named, prompt them to add nutrients, water and the carbon dioxide/waste the blood also carries.
activities.intendedInsight: The route forms a closed, continuous loop; the heart pumps and does not manufacture blood; capillaries link arteries to veins where exchange happens.
learnerActions: Put the blood's route in order: body → heart → lungs (collect oxygen) → heart → body.

Answer: if blood isn't used up, how does the same blood keep delivering oxygen all day? By what route does it get from your toes back to your heart? Besides oxygen, what else is it carrying as it passes your toes? Where does it pick up fresh oxygen?
Choose the correct statement and explain why 'blood only travels one way and gets used up' is wrong.
Describe the heart's job as pumping (not making) blood, noting blood cells are produced in bone marrow.
activities.title: Order the journey and check understanding

feedback: Keep the focus on 'two destinations' rather than full chamber-and-valve anatomy.
If chambers/valves come up, note these are explored in more detail at a later stage (KS3).
activities.intendedInsight: The heart is a genuinely three-dimensional muscular double pump with left and right sides feeding two destinations (lungs and body).
learnerActions: Examine a rotatable/cutaway model of the heart to see the left and right sides and how the great vessels connect.
Relate the left/right sides to the idea that the heart pumps blood to the lungs AND to the body.
activities.title: Enrichment: explore the heart in three dimensions
